nameStory: The 'bluntleaf' part of this bedstraw's name comes from its rounded leaf tips, which are notably less pointed than most of its bedstraw cousins. Like other bedstraws, it gets the 'bedstraw' name from the historical practice of stuffing dried plants from this family into mattresses and bedding, where they released a sweet, hay-like fragrance and helped repel insects.
description: Bluntleaf bedstraw is a delicate, low-growing wildflower that spreads along the ground or climbs weakly through other plants. It's a member of the madder family, related to coffee plants, and produces tiny white flowers in small clusters. This native plant typically stays under a foot tall, with slender stems that feel square when you roll them between your fingers. Its small, narrow leaves grow in circles around the stem, creating distinctive wheel-like patterns called whorls.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are arranged in whorls of 4-6 around the stem, but the key feature is their blunt, rounded tips rather than sharp points. They feel smooth and are quite narrow, almost needle-like but soft to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers, each only about 1/8 inch across, appear in small loose clusters. Each flower has four petals that spread flat like a little cross, giving them a delicate, star-like appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats or trails weakly through other vegetation, rarely standing upright on its own. The plant has a sprawling, almost creeping quality as it spreads along the ground.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender stems feel distinctly square when rolled between your fingers, a characteristic shared with other bedstraws. They're usually smooth and green, sometimes with a slightly reddish tinge.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, dry fruits that are smooth rather than hooked or bristly, unlike some of its grabby bedstraw relatives that stick to clothing.

habitat: Bluntleaf bedstraw prefers moist to wet areas, often found in marshes, wet meadows, and along the edges of ponds and streams. It thrives in areas with rich, organic soils and can tolerate both sunny and partially shaded locations. In New England, look for it in low-lying areas that stay consistently moist throughout the growing season.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with fresh green whorled leaves appearing on sprawling stems. The plant begins to form its characteristic low mats during late spring.
seasonality.summer: Blooming period occurs in mid to late summer, when the tiny white four-petaled flowers appear in delicate clusters. This is the best time for identification when flowers are present.
seasonality.fall: Flowers give way to small smooth fruits, and the plant may begin to turn yellowish or brown. The distinctive leaf arrangement remains visible until hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving little trace above soil level. Look for dried stems in protected areas, though identification is nearly impossible during dormant season.

funFact: Despite being in the same family as coffee plants, bluntleaf bedstraw and its relatives were actually used by early settlers as a coffee substitute during shortages - though the flavor was reportedly quite different from the real thing!
confusionNotes: With only 4 recorded observations in New England, bluntleaf bedstraw is easily confused with the much more common three-petal bedstraw and Common Marsh-bedstraw in wet areas. The key is those distinctly blunt, rounded leaf tips - run your finger along the leaves and you won't feel any sharp points, unlike most other bedstraws which have pointed leaf tips that can feel slightly prickly.
contextualKnowledge: Bluntleaf bedstraw is extremely rare in New England with only 4 documented observations, making it one of our region's most uncommon bedstraws. If you think you've found it, double-check your identification and consider reporting your sighting to local botanists, as new location records would be scientifically valuable.
compareHints: Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips. While Common Marsh-bedstraw also likes wet areas, its leaves come to sharp points. Three-petal bedstraw shares wet habitats but has even tinier flowers with only three petals instead of four, and pointed leaves that feel rough along the edges.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit.

Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles.
Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern.
Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms.
Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw).
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.

White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
